name: Radish
summary: How Filipino vegetable farmers usually grow long white labanos, sown straight on a well prepared field and pulled about 40 to 45 days later. For lowland and highland growers who want the usual routine and the few changes that give straight, white, heavy roots.
season: In the lowlands labanos does best in the cooler dry months, but growers in places like Laguna and Quezon plant it in both the dry and the wet season, choosing varieties that stand rain and do not bolt. In the highlands, such as Atok and Kibungan in Benguet, it is grown through most of the year.
material: Seed, broadcast over the field or sown in shallow rows. Open pollinated seed is cheap but farmers use more of it. Growers in Laguna report about 4 kg of open pollinated seed against about 2 kg of hybrid seed for a quarter hectare.
spacing: Most growers broadcast the seed over a well prepared field and thin crowded spots by hand. Others sow in shallow rows on beds and thin along the row so the roots do not touch.
water: Watered daily at first, by hand, sprinkler or furrow, then kept evenly moist. In the rainy season farmers plant on raised beds so water does not stand around the roots.
fertilizer: The traditional base is a lot of well rotted chicken manure spread before sowing. Urea goes on only while the plants are young. Experienced growers stop giving nitrogen at about 20 to 25 days, when the main root starts to form.
care: Daily watering in the first days, thinning of crowded spots, one or two hand weedings, and a single early side dressing of urea.
harvest: Long white labanos is ready about 40 to 45 days after sowing. Farmers pull the biggest roots first and go over the field in several rounds, then wash and sort the roots, keeping straight, smooth, white ones as first class.

steps.title: Plow and harrow until fine
steps.how: Plow and harrow the field thoroughly so the soil is deep, loose and free of clods and stones. Lumps and stones make forked, crooked roots.

steps.title: Spread rotted chicken manure
steps.how: Spread plenty of well rotted chicken manure over the field and mix it into the top soil. One Laguna grower uses about 60 sacks for half a hectare.
steps.tip: Never use fresh manure. It burns the seedlings and forks the roots.

steps.title: Broadcast the seed
steps.how: Scatter the seed as evenly as you can over the field or the beds, or drop it in shallow rows, then rake in lightly and water.

steps.title: Keep the soil moist
steps.how: Water every day until the seedlings are up, then keep the soil evenly moist. Dry spells followed by heavy watering make the roots crack.

steps.title: Thin crowded spots
steps.how: Pull out extra seedlings where they come up too close together so each root has room. The young plants can be cooked.

steps.title: Give urea early only
steps.how: Side dress with a little urea while the plants are young, before the main root starts to swell. Do not give urea or other nitrogen after about 20 days, or the plant makes leaves instead of root.

steps.title: Weed by hand
steps.how: Pull the weeds once or twice while the plants are small.

steps.title: Check leaves and roots
steps.how: Look for flea beetle holes, aphids and green caterpillars on the leaves, and for rotting at the root top in wet weather. Pull and remove rotting plants.

steps.title: Pull the roots in rounds
steps.how: From about 40 days, pull the biggest roots first and come back for the rest in later rounds. Most of the field is harvested by about 45 days.
steps.tip: Do not leave roots too long. They turn pithy, woody and hot tasting.

steps.title: Wash and sort
steps.how: Wash off the soil, sort the straight, smooth, white roots from the forked or cracked ones, and pack them in the shade for selling the same day or the next.

mistakes: Giving urea after the root starts to swell, so the plant grows leaves and a thin root.
Sowing on cloddy or stony soil, or with fresh manure, which makes forked roots.
Sowing too thick and never thinning, so the roots stay small and twisted.
Uneven watering that makes the roots crack.
Leaving the roots in the ground too long until they turn pithy and woody.
better: Use fresh seed of a variety suited to your season and elevation, with tolerance to rain and bolting.
Test the soil and lime sour soils. Feed with rotted manure plus balanced fertilizer by the result.
Prepare deep, fine, raised beds, especially in the rainy months.
Sow evenly and thin early so every root has room.
Rotate labanos with crops outside the cabbage family and keep the field clean of old roots.
Harvest on time and keep the roots shaded and cool after washing.

watering.traditional: Labanos is watered every day at first, by hand, sprinkler or furrow, until the seedlings are up, and then kept evenly moist until it is pulled. In the rainy season farmers plant on raised beds so water does not stand around the roots.
watering.method: Watering cans and hoses on small beds, sprinklers in the highlands, and furrows on bigger lowland fields. Water in the morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: In the rainy season labanos grows on raised beds with little watering. In the dry months it needs daily water at first, so without a pump keep the beds near a well and mulch with rice straw or rice hull.
watering.dryseason: Water every day until the seedlings are up, then about every day or two to keep the soil evenly moist, more on sandy soil. Water when the top soil is dry to the touch or the leaves droop by late morning.
watering.wet: Plant on raised beds so water does not stand around the roots, and skip watering in rainy weeks. Soaked soil rots the roots and splits them, and hard rain beats down the young leaves.

schedule.often: Water right after sowing, then every day until the seedlings are up
schedule.amount: A fine spray that keeps the top soil damp without washing the seed
schedule.why: The seed sits shallow and dies if the top soil dries.

schedule.often: Keep the soil evenly moist, about every day or two in dry weather. Water after thinning and after the early urea
schedule.amount: Even waterings that wet the bed to the roots
schedule.why: The root starts swelling early, and a dry week now makes it tough and hot tasting.

schedule.often: Keep the same even schedule, more often on sandy soil and in hot weather
schedule.amount: The same amount each time, never a dry spell followed by a heavy soaking
schedule.why: Dry spells followed by heavy watering make the roots crack, and dry soil makes them pithy and woody.

schedule.often: Keep watering lightly while pulling in rounds
schedule.why: Moist soil lets the roots come out whole and keeps the remaining ones crisp.

critical: Sowing to coming up: the top soil must stay damp.
Root swelling: even moisture, with no dry spells followed by soaking.

signs.dry: Leaves wilt in the heat, roots stay small, turn woody, pithy or very hot tasting, and plants flower early.
signs.wet: Roots split, turn soft or rot at the shoulder, and the leaves yellow.

better: Keep the watering even every day or two. It is the best guard against cracked and pithy roots.
Mulch the beds with rice straw or rice hull to hold moisture between waterings.
